whisper_segs.text: Good morning, it's 7 o'clock on Friday the 27th of February.
This is Morning Ireland on RTE Radio 1 with Gavin Jennings and Cian McCormack.
Today, can't pay, can't pay.
A big jump in people falling behind on their energy bills.
Also, Labour lose a Manchester election, Arman in Ukraine, the end of the wet winter and another Mayo lotto millionaire.
In business, Netflix walks away from its Warner Brothers takeover deal and we'll hear from Aer Lingus'CEO as the airline reports annual results.
In sport, heavy punishment for Drogheda United over their fans'behaviour in Dundalk and GA Congress meets to elect a new president.
Well, all that and more between now and nine o'clock.
But first, Sharon Lynch has the news.
There has been a sharp increase in the number of people in arrears with their energy bills.
The rise comes at a time of increased gas and electricity costs since the Russian invasion of Ukraine four years ago.
Figures published by the Commission for the Regulation of Utilities show that the number of people behind on their energy bills rose to almost 320,000
on December 2025, an increase of almost 20% on the previous year.
Joe Caulfield reports.
Year on year, the number of people unable to pay the whole of their energy bills rose from 264,458 in December 2024 to 319,459 last December.
The last two months of the year saw a significant jump from over 303,000 customers in November to almost 320,000 in December, a rise of over 5% month on month.
26% of all domestic gas customers were in arrears in December last year, with 14% of electricity customers unable to pay part or all of their bill.
In addition to an increase in the number of customers in arrears, the average amount owed by electricity customers increased by 10% year-on-year, although the amount owed by gas customers
fell by 1%.
Pakistan's Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has declared open war on the Taliban in Afghanistan.
Mr Asif said Pakistan's patience with the Taliban had reached its limit.
His statement followed a surge in clashes between the Pakistani military and Taliban forces.
Pakistani fighter jets have bombed several locations in Afghanistan, including the capital Kabul.
The Taliban claimed it had killed at least 10 Pakistani soldiers.
Pakistan said it had killed more than 70 Taliban combatants.
Pakistan has consistently accused the Taliban of sheltering militants who attack soldiers and civilians in Pakistan, an allegation the Taliban denies.
The Hamas-run health ministry in Gaza has said at least five people were killed in Israeli attacks on the Palestinian territory yesterday.
The international medical humanitarian organisation Doctors Without Borders has said a big influx of aid is urgently needed amid catastrophic conditions in Gaza.
It said lives continue to be lost because of sustained violence and persistent aid restrictions imposed by the Israeli authorities.
The governing Labour Party in Britain has lost a parliamentary by-election in its former stronghold of Gordon and Denton in north-west England.
The seat was won by the Green Party candidate, with the right-wing Reform Party pushing the Labour Party candidate into third place.

Period.

The paper says that because of government rules, it won't pay a cent of stamp duty on them.

That's in the mail.
A few pages over, a story that appears in several papers, head straps for babies.
The paper says that parents have been warned that putting a head strap on a baby's forehead in the car can be dangerous.
People use them to stop their baby's heads from slumping forwards or to the side when they fall asleep, but there's a danger they could slip down and strangle or suffocate the baby.
The Mail says these head straps have already been withdrawn from sale in Germany, Australia and Malta.

The woman he crashed into gave a victim impact statement in court.
She told the judge that she was 31 weeks pregnant at the time and when she woke up in hospital, she was told that she had lost her baby.
She later found out that her unborn baby would not be recorded as a separate baby.
She said, I'm aware that no sentence can undo what happened.

Recognition matters.
Acknowledgement of the full harm caused matters, not only to me, but to my family and to the memory of my son.

It tells us that every inch of the N40 is the site of a crash.
The paper says this was a comment to a local community safety partnership lately.

He wants a constant guard of presence on the N40, both to improve driver behaviour and to clear collisions quickly.

Good morning, Tony.
Morning, Cian.
Kharkiv, close to the border with Russia.
It's really at the coalface in this conflict.
What's happening there this morning?
That's right, Cian.

And Kharkiv is...
It's a location of shifting identities over the ages.
You know, it's a...
a very Russian city, if you like, a Russophone, Russified over the decades.
But since the invasion four years ago, sentiment has sharply turned against Moscow.

That's reflected in sentiment here, people that you talk to, but also the fact that Kharkiv has been particularly, and some would say vindictively punished by Russia for trying to resist the invasion in 2022.
There were 300 attacks last year against the city, and that seems to be continuing at the moment.
There are daily drone and missile attacks on infrastructure and on residential blocks here.
And also drones are getting closer, drones that are fired from the Russian Federation, getting closer to Kharkiv all the time.
These are fiber optic drones, which are very hard to jam.
And as a result, the authorities are having to build.
Corridors covered by nets on major highways around the city.
There's an 18-kilometre stretch of road that has been covered in netting.
These are like fishing nets to try and prevent drones hitting civilian vehicles or obviously military vehicles as well.
So it does still feel like a city under siege.
Much of life happens underground, schooling, culture, and the population here are simply trying to endure the war as it enters its fifth year.
Those nets, Tony, how surreal is that to witness?
It's very surreal given the manpower involved.
I met a team yesterday using scaffolding on wheels to erect these nets.
They line metal poles, iron poles along the side of the road for one kilometre after another.
And then they hoist up nets that are suspended over the road.
Now, these can be effective.
They are hard to penetrate by drones.
France and Spain has been providing fishing nets to help Ukraine.
The government is rolling out here a whole program of thousands of kilometers of netting that would have to be erected in key cities that are subject to drone attacks.
And that's just the nature of this war.
It's all about adaptation and ingenuity.
And that's really where things are at at the moment.
But as you say, Tony, Kharkiv, it seems itself has been vindictively punished.
Now, four years on, what's the mood like there?
I think it's one of defiance and one of survival.
Day to day, you know, there are regularly attacks on apartment blocks.
We went to one block yesterday that was hit by a Shahid drone at about eight minutes to four in the morning.
No obvious reason why this building should be targeted.
There was a huge hole in the gable wall of the apartment block and windows.
Shattered and immediately the routine kicks into gear.
You have the red cross.
Officer here, you have the police come and take statements and the whole process of registering the attack and helping the people there find alternative accommodation.
There's a whole system of bringing chipboard.
Blocks of wood or sheets of wood that can be put up to cover windows that are blown out.
This is happening every day, but there's a whole system in place to cope with that.
So I think the city feels that it is adapting, it's resilient, and it's just trying to get on with life.
And, you know, a lot of the activity here has returned to some kind of normality compared to what it was like four years ago when the war was raging.
And that's the daily life during war is the impact on people and then more trilateral talks on the cards.
What way are people in Harkiv viewing those talks potentially?
I mean, people are generally sceptical about Russia's intentions.
Now, of course, they want the war to end.
Nobody wants the war to end more than the people of Kharkiv and Ukraine.
But the opinion polls in general in Ukraine show that a very large majority of people would prefer the war to continue rather than a peace which amounts to capitulation.
And there is a sense four years on that the country is stronger, it's more united, it's more resolute, and it has pulled together in an extremely effective way.

if you like, even if there has been a colossal sacrifice in terms of the thousands of dead civilians, tens of thousands, perhaps hundreds of thousands of soldiers dead, cities razed to the ground, infrastructure destroyed.

Talks at official level between Ukrainian and American teams in Geneva.
